name: Extraordinary Claims Rule
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Sagan's Rule: Why Big Claims Need Big Evidence
lesson.summary: Carl Sagan's famous standard, that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, is not a slogan but a direct consequence of base rate reasoning: the more a claim would overturn what we already have strong reason to believe, the lower its starting probability, and the more evidence it takes to justify believing it anyway.
lesson.body:
The astronomer Carl Sagan popularized a simple standard for evaluating dramatic claims: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. It is often repeated as a slogan, but it is really a precise, logical statement, and the previous chapter on base rate reasoning already gave you the machinery to understand exactly why it works. A claim is extraordinary not because it sounds exciting, but because it has a low base rate given everything else we already have good reason to believe. An extraordinary claim is one that would require overturning well established results, beating very long odds, or achieving something that essentially everyone with relevant expertise currently believes is still far away.

Recall the disease test example: a rare condition, a 1 percent base rate, needed strong, well calibrated evidence to overcome the odds against it, and a single ordinary test result was nowhere near enough on its own, it only moved belief to about 16.7 percent, still more likely false than true. The same logic scales up. If a claim's base rate is even lower, for instance a claim that a small team solved the decoherence problem outright, or that a fully useful, large scale quantum computer already exists years ahead of every public roadmap, then a single demo, a single press release, or a single unreplicated paper is the equivalent of one positive test on a rare condition: interesting, worth following up on, and nowhere close to sufficient on its own.

So what actually counts as extraordinary evidence in practice? Independent replication by researchers with no stake in the outcome. Peer review with published methodology that others can actually check. The ability of other labs to reproduce the result rather than take it on faith. Converging evidence from multiple independent groups rather than one team's account of its own work. And concrete, falsifiable numbers rather than vague superlative language. A claim like a quantum computer has broken widely used encryption would need essentially all of these before it should shift anyone's beliefs significantly. A claim like a team improved qubit coherence time by 10 percent in a specific narrow system is a much more ordinary claim, well within the normal pace of incremental progress, and does not require anywhere near the same evidentiary bar.

It is worth guarding against a common misuse of the rule. Sagan's standard is not a license to dismiss anything ambitious as automatically false, and treating it that way turns a calibration tool into a thought terminating reflex, which is its own kind of miscalibration. The rule does not say extraordinary claims are always wrong, it says the amount of evidence required scales with how much the claim would need to overturn. Applying it well is an active practice, not a party trick, and it is the second tool in this course's toolkit, right alongside base rate reasoning, for meeting any dramatic quantum computing claim you will encounter from here on.
